Jaguar XKSS: Beauty Born of Speed

The most beautiful Jaguar ever made? The E-Type may have captured the world’s imagination, but the XKSS was something rarer, more purposeful, and arguably more extraordinary. Born from a Le Mans champion, nearly erased by fire, and immortalized by Steve McQueen, it remains one of the greatest expressions of what a sports car can be.

By Elliot Vance · 28 minute read

The Jaguar That Needed No Introduction

There is a photograph of Steve McQueen sitting behind the wheel of his Jaguar XKSS. He looks perfectly at home, which is remarkable, because the car itself looks as though it has absolutely no business being on a public road. The windshield is almost an afterthought. The front fenders rise dramatically from a body so low that the driver appears to be sitting inside the pavement, and beneath the passenger door a long exhaust pipe emerges from the bodywork like the barrel of a weapon. It is exquisite.

What makes the image so compelling is not simply the presence of Hollywood’s most celebrated automotive enthusiast. It is the realization that McQueen, a man who could afford almost anything, chose to spend so much of his time in a car that made virtually no concessions to comfort, convenience, or ordinary human expectations. He called it the Green Rat. This was no pampered grand tourer for pleasant afternoons on the Pacific Coast Highway. It was a racing machine with license plates, a roof that barely deserved the name, and enough performance to embarrass some of the finest sports cars of its day.

There are beautiful automobiles. There are legendary racing cars. And there are a very few machines that seem to transcend both categories. The Jaguar XKSS belongs to that last group. Only 16 were completed in Jaguar’s original 1957 program. It was born from the D-Type, a car that conquered the 24 Hours of Le Mans 3 consecutive times. It survived one of the most devastating fires in British automotive history, went on to win races across North America, and eventually became one of the most desirable collector cars in existence.

Yet none of this quite explains its appeal. The XKSS possesses a quality very few automobiles ever achieve: it seems inevitable, as though someone removed everything unnecessary from a sports car until only the essential beauty remained. That is a strange and wonderful thing, because the XKSS was never really designed to be beautiful at all. It was designed to be fast.

Before the XKSS, There Was Le Mans

To understand the XKSS, we have to go back to the early 1950s, when Jaguar was transforming itself from an accomplished British sports-car maker into an international racing powerhouse. The XK120 had already shown that Jaguar could build a genuinely fast road car at a comparatively accessible price, and the C-Type then established the company’s engineering credibility on the most demanding endurance circuits in the world. The C-Type won Le Mans in 1951 and again in 1953, and that second victory helped prove the superiority of disc brakes under the punishing demands of a 24-hour race.

But Jaguar wanted more. Its engineers understood that the next great leap would not necessarily come from adding horsepower. At Le Mans, and particularly along the seemingly endless Mulsanne Straight, cutting aerodynamic drag could be worth just as much.

Enter Malcolm Sayer. Sayer was not an ordinary automotive stylist. He had come to Jaguar from the Bristol Aeroplane Company, and he approached car design with the analytical discipline of an aerodynamicist. His understanding of airflow, structural efficiency, and mathematical form shaped Jaguar’s racing cars at the most fundamental level. Where other manufacturers sculpted bodywork around an existing chassis, Sayer considered how the entire machine could move through the air. The result was the D-Type.

Introduced in 1954, it was unlike nearly anything else on the grid. Its long, impossibly low hood blended into voluptuous front fenders, a small oval mouth fed the engine, and the body narrowed toward a cockpit set deep within a lightweight structure. Its most distinctive feature was its aircraft-inspired construction. Rather than relying on a conventional full-length chassis, Jaguar used a riveted light-alloy central monocoque, with a tubular frame up front carrying the engine and suspension. It was sophisticated, light, and exceptionally strong for its era. Jaguar’s magnificent twin-cam XK straight-six was mounted at an angle to lower the hood line, and dry-sump lubrication let it sit lower still. Disc brakes on all 4 wheels supplied the stopping power to survive a race in which the cars accelerated again and again to tremendous speeds before braking hard for corners.

And then there was the shape. It was no accident that the D-Type looked like something capable of flight.

In 1954, the new Jaguar finished second at Le Mans, narrowly missing victory on its debut. In 1955, Mike Hawthorn and Ivor Bueb took the D-Type to its first Le Mans win, in a race forever overshadowed by the catastrophic accident that killed more than 80 spectators. In 1956, the Scottish privateer team Ecurie Ecosse won with Ron Flockhart and Ninian Sanderson. Then came 1957. With Jaguar’s factory team withdrawn after the previous season, privately entered D-Types simply took over: Ecurie Ecosse won again, this time with Flockhart and Bueb, and D-Types filled 5 of the first 6 places.

That made 3 consecutive Le Mans victories, and not 3 for the same team, but 3 for the same extraordinary machine. By the standards of the 1950s, the D-Type represented a profound convergence of engineering, speed, and visual elegance. Yet Jaguar was about to do something even more extraordinary. It would make the D-Type a road car.

A Racer Pretending to Be a Sports Car

The familiar story of the XKSS begins with an awkward commercial reality. Jaguar had withdrawn from factory racing at the end of 1956, leaving a number of D-Type chassis unsold, and those cars represented a considerable investment in engineering and manufacturing. Sir William Lyons, Jaguar’s co-founder and a famously shrewd businessman, recognized an opportunity. Why not turn these racing cars into road-going sports cars for customers, particularly wealthy American enthusiasts who wanted something considerably more exciting than the usual showroom offerings?

There was another motivation. Jaguar’s competition chief, Lofty England, later explained that the Sports Car Club of America would not accept the D-Type as a production-based sports car, road-legal construction or not. Give the car a recognizable identity as a production road car, and that problem might go away. So the XKSS was never simply an exercise in clearing unwanted inventory. It also served a competition purpose, although it would be misleading to say Jaguar built it solely to satisfy one homologation rule. The honest answer is a mixture of commercial pragmatism, customer demand, and racing ambition.

What makes the decision so audacious is how little Jaguar needed to change. The towering fin and headrest fairing behind the driver disappeared, along with the bar that divided the cockpit. A proper passenger door was fitted. A full-width windshield with wipers replaced the racing screen, joined by removable side screens, a rudimentary folding top, and a small luggage rack on the tail. Slim chrome bumperettes appeared at both ends. The car picked up modest concessions to ordinary motoring, but no one could seriously accuse Jaguar of making it conventional. The tub, the front frame, the engine, the gearbox, the rear axle, the suspension, the brakes, the steering, and most of the bodywork stayed exactly as they were. In mechanical terms, this was not a sports car inspired by a racer.

It was a racer pretending to be a sports car.

For 1957, that was an almost outrageous proposition. The prototype, converted in Jaguar’s experimental department from D-Type XKD 555, was finished on January 14, 1957, and was on its way to America 4 days later. It carried a list price of $6,900, about $83,000 in 2026 money, and the plan called for 25 cars.

February 12, 1957

Then, on the evening of February 12, disaster struck. A fire that started in a tire bay tore through the Browns Lane factory in Coventry, spreading through buildings full of materials, equipment, and hundreds of cars. Employees fought to save what they could, but the damage was devastating. The XKSS program ended that night at 16 cars. The 9 still in progress never left the building finished. The usual telling says all 9 burned; some histories say several were damaged and broken up for parts afterward. Either way, none was ever completed, and the jigs needed to build more were lost too. In a matter of hours, a rare automobile became something approaching mythical, and the XKSS lost any chance to grow into the modest production series Jaguar had envisioned.

The 16 survivors scattered: 14 went to North America, 1 to Hong Kong, and 1 stayed in Britain. There is an important footnote, too. Jaguar later converted 2 more D-Types to XKSS specification, bringing the broader count of period factory cars to 18, though collectors still draw a firm line between those later conversions and the celebrated original 16.

Nearly 6 decades later, Jaguar Classic returned to the story, and it chose its stage with care. On November 16, 2016, the first newly built XKSS in almost 60 years, finished in Sherwood Green, was unveiled at the Petersen Automotive Museum in Los Angeles, the same building that holds McQueen’s Green Rat. That was 10 years ago this month. Jaguar kept that car as its reference and went on to build 9 continuation cars for customers, carrying chassis numbers from the original log, to complete the run of 25. Built from historical drawings, digital scans of surviving cars, and traditional craftsmanship, at an estimated 10,000 hours apiece, they sold for more than £1 million each, quoted in the United States at about $1.5 million (around $2.1 million in 2026). They are astonishing exercises in recreating an automotive masterpiece. But they were not built in 1957, and that distinction matters. The original XKSS is a survivor of an industrial tragedy, a genuine piece of racing history, and a car whose scarcity was shaped as much by circumstance as by intention. Sometimes history creates legends that no marketing department could ever invent.

The Case for the Most Beautiful Jaguar Ever Made

The conventional answer to the question of Jaguar’s most beautiful car is the E-Type, and it is not hard to see why. Introduced in 1961, the E-Type caused an international sensation. Its elongated hood, low stance, covered headlamps, and graceful fastback or open-roadster bodywork became shorthand for automotive beauty. It was glamorous, comparatively attainable, and built in substantial numbers over a 14-year production life. It became the Jaguar everyone knew. Yet the XKSS had beaten it to the road by 4 years. In his book Dream Cars, Andrew Frankel calls the XKSS a largely forgotten Jaguar despite being “faster and better bred” than its world-famous successor, and he lays the forgetting at the door of the fire.

But familiarity and beauty are not the same thing. The XKSS is arguably the more compelling piece of design precisely because it was never meant for widespread consumption. Its proportions are more radical. The front fenders swell over the wheels with almost muscular exaggeration, yet the narrow center body seems to disappear between them. The hood is startlingly low, the rear deck tightly drawn, and the cockpit so compact that the whole car appears to have been built around the driver’s shoulders. Its little chrome bumpers look almost apologetic.

The side-exit exhaust is particularly wonderful. It is not disguised or concealed, because concealing it would serve no purpose. The solid Dunlop light-alloy wheels, each held on by a single knock-off spinner, add another layer of mechanical honesty. Jaguar chose them over wire wheels as much for stiffness as for lightness, and the holes near the rims are there to let the brakes breathe. And unlike many glamorous automobiles of the period, the XKSS does not lean on ornament to establish its character. Its beauty comes from engineering. Every curve has a job.

The D-Type underneath was developed to minimize drag, shrink frontal area, improve stability, and survive the demands of endurance racing. The XKSS kept that essential form while losing the visually dominant competition fin, and the result is, to these eyes, even more seductive. Where the E-Type is elegant, the XKSS is elemental. The E-Type looks like a sports car imagined by an artist. The XKSS looks like a sports car discovered by an engineer who happened to possess the soul of an artist, and in Malcolm Sayer, Jaguar had precisely that combination.

Would the E-Type be universally regarded as Jaguar’s greatest design if the XKSS had been built in the thousands rather than 16? Perhaps. Or perhaps scarcity is part of what makes the XKSS so mesmerizing. One thing is certain: the XKSS deserves to be discussed alongside the E-Type rather than as an obscure footnote to the D-Type’s racing career. It is one of the most extraordinary examples of functional automotive beauty ever created.

The Drive: A Racing Car That Never Learned to Behave

It is easy to admire the XKSS as sculpture and forget just how violently fast it was. Under that long, low hood sat Jaguar’s 3,442 cc XK straight-six, with twin overhead camshafts, 2 valves per cylinder, and 3 Weber carburetors. In road-going form its output was commonly quoted at about 250 horsepower, and Road & Track credited its test car with 260. Today, 250 horsepower is not a dramatic number. In 1957, in a car weighing about 914 kg (2,015 lb) by Jaguar’s figure (some references go as high as 1,050 kg, or 2,315 lb), it was astonishing.

A 4-speed manual gearbox sent the power to the rear wheels. The front suspension used independent double wishbones and torsion bars, while the rear kept a live axle located by trailing links and a torsion bar. Rack-and-pinion steering connected driver to road, and disc brakes at all 4 corners gave it stopping power many rivals could only envy.

The XKSS could reach 60 mph from rest in about 5 seconds. Figures from 4.7 to 5.5 seconds have been quoted, and on narrow 1950s racing tires it was traction, not the gearbox, that set the limit. Top-speed figures vary with gearing, conditions, and source, landing between about 140 and 150 mph, and no official top-speed run was ever made to settle the argument. The racing D-Type’s often-quoted speeds approaching 180 mph cannot simply be transferred to the road car, because the full windshield and the loss of the racing aerodynamics changed its behavior at very high speed. Even with that qualification, the performance was spectacular.

Consider the contradiction. This was an open 2-seater with a folding top and license plates, and it had enough acceleration to trouble genuinely exotic machinery decades after its introduction. In 1957, plenty of family sedans struggled to see 90 mph, and Jaguar’s own XK150 road car needed nearly twice as long to reach 60. The XKSS was a glimpse of a future in which racing-car performance could be enjoyed on public roads, a future the rest of the industry had barely begun to imagine.

So what did it actually feel like? The temptation is to picture an impossibly raw and temperamental machine, fit only for professional racing drivers and fearless enthusiasts. Contemporary road tests and later firsthand accounts reveal something more interesting. The XKSS was unquestionably demanding, yet its sophistication made it far more usable than its appearance suggests.

The first surprise was the engine. Jaguar’s straight-six was already celebrated for its smoothness and flexibility, and even in racing trim it had real breadth. When Road & Track tested an XKSS in August 1957, its testers found the engine idling contentedly at around 700 rpm and then coming fully alive at about 3,500, with second gear so eager that over-revving was easy. At 100 mph the car felt so relaxed it seemed to be doing 50. Frankel reckons it was docile enough to run errands in without a murmur of protest. That mattered. A road-going racing car that could not cope with ordinary driving would be little more than a novelty, and the XKSS was something more complete.

Yet it never concealed its origins. The same test found the passenger’s legroom a foot short of adequate and the toe-boards miserably hot, because the exhaust ran directly beneath them. The racing generator also charged so lazily that the battery needed frequent recharging. As for the noise, R&T judged the exhaust “much too loud for legal driving in most areas.” The growl of the engine, the pipe running just below the cockpit, the low seating position, and the sparse interior made every journey an event.

The steering was another revelation. Modern performance cars filter road information through power assistance, electronics, and layers of refinement. The XKSS had no interest in such things. Its rack-and-pinion steering provided a direct mechanical connection to the front wheels, so the driver felt what the tires were doing, how the nose loaded into a corner, and how the car answered every change of direction.

Frankel drove the original XKSS prototype at Goodwood for Motor Sport in 2015. He admired its dials, the view down that long hood, and the engine’s growl, and above all he came away describing a car that pours information from the road straight into the driver. He also noted a slight stumble at low revs and part throttle, which he put down to the freshly restored car’s carburetor setup. That perhaps explains its lasting appeal better than any performance statistic. The XKSS was not simply fast. It made speed feel meaningful.

Where It Shined

The car’s greatest strengths were its immediacy, balance, and sense of connection. A short wheelbase, low weight, and precise steering made changes of direction feel direct and purposeful. Its brakes were genuinely advanced for the era, and drivers accustomed to fading drums would have found the Jaguar’s discs immensely reassuring. Its power-to-weight ratio made acceleration out of corners electrifying, and its D-Type chassis had been developed to stay composed at speeds that would have exposed the weaknesses of lesser automobiles. Frankel writes that it would hold a slide on the throttle, neatly balanced, at better than 100 mph.

None of this means the XKSS was effortless. The live rear axle could become unsettled on rough surfaces, particularly when the driver changed throttle or brake inputs abruptly. The narrow racing-derived tires offered far less ultimate grip than modern performance rubber. The 4-speed gearbox, Frankel notes, is easier to work than its oddly laid-back lever suggests, but there were no electronic aids to rescue a poor decision. Brake hard after hard acceleration and the weight pitched forward, lightening the rear tires and making the car nervous. This was not a vehicle that rewarded clumsy inputs. It asked the driver to understand weight transfer, tire adhesion, and the rhythm of the road.

On fast, sweeping corners and relatively smooth surfaces, its racing heritage gave it exceptional composure. On broken, uneven roads, the short wheelbase, firm suspension, and live rear axle demanded considerably more attention. And that, perhaps, is part of its brilliance. The XKSS did not make a mediocre driver feel like a racing hero. It gave a talented driver the tools to become one.

A Mechanical Conversation

Picture it. A long, sweeping corner opens up ahead and the road falls away from you. The engine settles into a purposeful growl as you ease off the throttle and lean on the brakes, and the nose answers immediately. You turn the wood-rimmed wheel and feel the front tires load up through the steering rack, a running report from the road with nothing in between. The car takes a set, the live axle follows, and every shift of weight comes up through the seat. Then you feed in the power. The straight-six answers at once, the exhaust hardening into a metallic bark, and the Jaguar surges out of the bend with that long hood parting the air and you sitting almost entirely exposed to all of it.

That is what makes the XKSS special. A modern performance car would cover the same road more quickly, more safely, and with far less effort. The XKSS would make you remember every yard.

Steve McQueen and the Green Rat

Few automobiles are so perfectly tied to a single owner. Steve McQueen’s XKSS, chassis 713, was originally finished in off-white with a red interior. Before McQueen bought it in 1958, it belonged to James Edward Peterson, the man who designed Riverside Raceway, and then to television personality Bill Leyden. McQueen wanted the car to reflect his own taste. He had it repainted British Racing Green, had the Dunlop wheels polished, and commissioned the celebrated upholsterer Tony Nancy to replace the red interior with black leather. With its deep green paint, bright wheels, and dark cabin, the car took on a more purposeful, understated look, and McQueen christened it the Green Rat. It was an affectionate name, and a wonderfully irreverent one for an automobile that would become one of the world’s most valuable Jaguars.

McQueen was not interested in treating the XKSS as a delicate collector’s item. He drove it, frequently and by all accounts rather enthusiastically. The Green Rat became a familiar sight around Los Angeles, used for ordinary transportation, for trips to the studio, and for runs along the winding roads above the city. According to the Petersen Automotive Museum, all that enthusiasm earned him considerable attention from law enforcement: in his first year with the Jaguar, his traffic tickets reportedly put his license in jeopardy twice. Road & Track had warned everyone about that exhaust. This was a genuine racing machine in the hands of a man who loved driving as much as he loved acting, and for McQueen the XKSS was never a trophy. It was an experience.

Steve McQueen, Von Dutch, and a Pair of Flying Sunglasses

For all its brilliance, the XKSS apparently had one particularly annoying habit: it could not keep Steve McQueen’s sunglasses in place. Jaguar’s engineers had spent years perfecting the aerodynamics, chassis construction, and performance of the D-Type. They had considered airflow at close to 180 mph, the demands of endurance racing, and the strength of that revolutionary light-alloy structure. Designing a convenient place to keep sunglasses had not exactly been a priority.

The XKSS had an open storage cubby in its dashboard. Under ordinary circumstances, that might have been perfectly adequate. Under Steve McQueen’s circumstances, it was considerably less successful. As the story goes, whenever he drove the Jaguar with real enthusiasm, his sunglasses had a habit of launching themselves out of that open cubby. Hard acceleration, abrupt braking, and fast corners were apparently more than the arrangement could handle.

McQueen turned to his friend Kenneth Howard, better known as Von Dutch. Today the name is associated with custom-car culture and with the fashion brand that later adopted it, but Howard himself was a gifted pinstriper, metalworker, and customizer whose influence on American hot-rodding was considerable, and he had exactly the kind of ingenuity McQueen appreciated. Rather than redesign the dashboard or bolt on some elaborate accessory, Von Dutch fabricated a simple metal glovebox door. The new panel kept the sunglasses safely contained, even when the Green Rat was being driven the way its racing ancestry encouraged. It was an elegantly practical solution to a wonderfully ridiculous problem. Jaguar had built a car capable of competing at Le Mans, and Steve McQueen had discovered that its dashboard could not cope with a pair of sunglasses. There is something particularly charming about that contradiction.

More importantly, the modification reveals how McQueen regarded his cars. He did not approach the XKSS as a historically significant artifact that had to remain untouched. He regarded it as his car, something to be used, enjoyed, and improved when necessary, even when the car in question was one of the rarest Jaguars ever built. The Von Dutch glovebox door is still on chassis 713 today, a small piece of automotive history that perhaps captures the relationship between McQueen and the Green Rat better than anything else.

The World’s Most Extraordinary School Run

The Green Rat was also part of the McQueen family’s everyday life. The photographer William Claxton once caught a 3-year-old Chad McQueen on his tricycle in front of it, and Chad later remembered being driven to school in the Jaguar as a small boy, and his father driving it to the studio regularly for a time. Imagine being a young child in Los Angeles in the early 1960s, climbing into the passenger seat of a road-going Le Mans car while your father gets ready to take you to school. The door closes. The 6-cylinder bursts into life. The exhaust, running along the passenger side just below you, announces your departure to everyone within earshot. And off you go, not to a racing circuit, not to a prestigious concours, but to school.

These were ordinary journeys made extraordinary by the machine involved. Today the idea of an original XKSS as daily transportation seems almost absurd, since its rarity and value make it one of the most carefully protected automobiles in the world. But that was not how McQueen experienced it. He knew the Jaguar as a living, breathing machine. It was not an investment that happened to have wheels. It was a car woven into the rhythm of his life.

The One That Got Away, and Came Back

Like many enthusiasts, McQueen sometimes parted with cars he later regretted selling, and the XKSS was one of them. He eventually sold the Green Rat to casino owner and renowned collector William Harrah, on the understanding that it would be displayed in Harrah’s collection in Reno rather than driven or sold. Why let it go at all? The late Chad McQueen once asked his father exactly that, and the answer was that he was worried “something might break and kill him.”

The Jaguar stayed on his mind anyway. By Chad’s account, McQueen had sold it believing he could buy it back at the same price. Harrah, whose collection was by then in full swing, wanted more, and the haggling dragged on for a couple of years. In the late 1970s McQueen finally got his car back, and the Green Rat stayed with him until his death in 1980.

That decision is particularly revealing. McQueen owned an enviable range of automobiles and motorcycles, machinery from some of the world’s most celebrated manufacturers, and yet the XKSS was the one he felt compelled to recover. It had become something more than an exciting automobile. It was part of his history.

In 1984 the Green Rat sold at auction for $148,000 (about $481,000 in 2026) to Richard Freshman, McQueen’s friend and former neighbor, who had it sympathetically restored by Lynx in England with McQueen’s changes preserved, Tony Nancy’s leather and Von Dutch’s door included. Today it lives in the collection of the Petersen Automotive Museum in Los Angeles, a fitting home for a machine so deeply tied to Southern California’s car culture, and the building Jaguar chose a decade ago when it brought the XKSS back to life. Its association with McQueen has undoubtedly added to its fame. But perhaps the most important part of the story is not that a Hollywood legend owned an XKSS. It is that a man who could own almost anything kept choosing to drive one.

The Company It Kept

Did the XKSS actually win races? Absolutely, and it is one of the most overlooked parts of the story. The XKSS was not merely a road-going tribute to the D-Type’s achievements. Individual cars went racing, mostly in North America, and they won. The Racing Sports Cars archive records 166 entries for cars running as XKSSs between 1957 and 1964, 128 of them in the United States and 33 in Canada, with 28 outright wins and 15 more class wins. Those totals deserve some care, since period entries sometimes lack chassis numbers and cars were switched between D-Type and XKSS bodywork, but the broad conclusion is unmistakable. The XKSS was raced, and it won.

The prototype itself, XKSS 701, was the first in America, and Dave Tallaksen lined it up on the front row at Eagle Mountain, Texas, in April 1957 with little more preparation than taking the top off. In John Gordon Bennett’s hands it won at Mansfield, Louisiana, and Bob Stonedale of Houston campaigned it through 1959, reportedly with a Chevrolet V8 under the hood by the end. In Canada, Stan McRobert took XKSS 716 to 11 wins from 12 starts in 1957 and 1958 at St. Eugene and Harewood Acres. On the West Coast, Sidney Colberg of San Francisco was a regular at the tracks in XKSS 707 through the 1960s.

The Le Mans victories belong to the D-Type, not the XKSS. But the XKSS kept so much of the D-Type’s mechanical identity that the distinction is almost philosophical. Jaguar had built a road car that could compete on Sunday and be driven home afterward, and for enthusiasts in 1957 that was an irresistible proposition.

The XKSS did not arrive in a world short of great automobiles. The 1950s produced some of the most significant sports cars ever built, and the Jaguar faced formidable competition from Germany, Italy, Britain, and America. Each approached the idea of a high-performance road car differently, and the numbers show just how differently.

The Mercedes-Benz 300 SL Roadster was the XKSS’s closest philosophical rival. Introduced in 1957 to succeed the celebrated Gullwing, it paired an advanced fuel-injected 3.0-liter straight-six with excellent high-speed ability and far more road-going refinement. Its 215 to 222 horsepower, depending on the measurement standard, was impressive. But at roughly 1,330 kg (2,932 lb), it carried more than 400 kg (880 lb) more than the Jaguar, and it cost more too, at $10,950 against the Jaguar’s $6,900 (about $131,500 and $82,900 in 2026). Where the XKSS was a barely domesticated racing car, the 300 SL Roadster was a sophisticated high-performance touring machine, with better weather protection, more comfort, and a more relaxed long-distance character. The Jaguar answered with a more immediate connection between driver and machine, less weight, and more ferocious acceleration. Both were brilliant, but the XKSS was the more uncompromising automobile.

Ferrari’s 250 GT family came at the idea from another direction. Its magnificent Colombo V12 was the centerpiece, offering a character and sound that Jaguar’s straight-six could not replicate, and the 250 GT models combined genuine sporting ability with the luxury, craftsmanship, and visual drama of an Italian grand tourer. Some versions, like the long-wheelbase Tour de France berlinettas, were formidable competition cars, while others were built mainly for fast continental travel. The famed short-wheelbase 250 GT would not appear until 1959. The XKSS, by contrast, was much closer to a pure racing machine: lighter, more elemental, and less interested in the comforts expected of a grand tourer. A Ferrari 250 GT might be the better companion for crossing Europe. The XKSS would make the journey feel like a qualifying session.

The Aston Martin DB Mark III, also new in 1957, was a distinctly British take on the sporting grand tourer, with handsome bodywork, a refined 6-cylinder engine, and a carefully appointed interior. Its standard 162 horsepower sat well below the XKSS’s output, though higher-performance versions narrowed the gap. The Aston was meant to be driven quickly and comfortably over long distances, while the Jaguar was meant to make the driver feel every mile. The DB Mark III had considerable elegance. The XKSS had something closer to urgency.

Across the Atlantic, the 1957 Corvette was becoming a serious performance machine. Chevrolet’s new Rochester mechanical fuel injection allowed the most powerful version of its 283-cubic-inch small-block V8 to claim 283 horsepower, a landmark for an American production sports car. The Corvette was powerful, cheap by exotic-car standards at about $3,660 with fuel injection (around $44,000 in 2026), and increasingly capable in competition. But it was also substantially heavier than the Jaguar, at about 1,292 kg (2,849 lb), and it kept a far more conventional chassis. The Corvette offered enormous performance for the money. The XKSS offered an entirely different engineering philosophy: less mass, greater aerodynamic sophistication, and the mechanical DNA of an endurance-racing champion. Together they show just how differently manufacturers could chase the same thing.

Jaguar likes to point out that experts call the XKSS the world’s first supercar. It is an appealing claim, and there is a compelling argument behind it. The XKSS offered staggering performance, advanced engineering, visual drama, exclusivity, and a direct line to top-level motorsport, and it did so before the Lamborghini Miura, before the Ferrari 250 GTO, and long before supercars became a recognized marketing category. But automotive history rarely lends itself to simple firsts. The Mercedes-Benz 300 SL, introduced in coupe form in 1954, had already demonstrated supercar-level performance and technical sophistication, and other exotic limited-production automobiles came before the XKSS as well. Calling it definitively the world’s first supercar asks for more certainty than the historical record provides. Calling it one of the earliest and purest expressions of the supercar idea is entirely justified.

Indeed, the XKSS may represent something even more special. It is one of the earliest examples of a genuine top-level racing car being adapted for wealthy enthusiasts who wanted its performance on ordinary roads, with little compromise and almost no attempt to hide the competition engineering underneath. In that respect, it feels astonishingly modern. Its philosophy would later be echoed by generations of track-focused road cars, from homologation specials to modern Porsche GT machinery. But few have ever looked quite so magnificent.

The Value of Something Almost Irreplaceable

As collector cars grew into a market measured in millions, the XKSS naturally became one of Jaguar’s most coveted creations, and its appeal goes well beyond rarity. It combines racing ancestry, innovative engineering, exceptional design, genuine period competition history, and an astonishingly small surviving population. Put the numbers side by side. New in 1957, an XKSS listed at $6,900, about $83,000 in 2026 money, which made it cheaper than either a Mercedes-Benz 300 SL Roadster or an Aston Martin DB Mark III. In August 2023, an original 1957 XKSS, chassis 707, sold at RM Sotheby’s Monterey auction for $13,205,000 including buyer’s premium. That is about $14.5 million in 2026 money, and it was a record for the model at the time.

That car was a highly original, well-preserved example that still had its original engine block and cylinder head, gearbox, rear axle, and bodywork, along with a documented history of West Coast racing. It had been ordered new by the racer Lou Brero Sr., who was killed in a crash before he could take delivery. It had also taken part in the 2022 Colorado Grand, proof that at least some owners still regard these automobiles as machines to be driven rather than static investments.

The sale illustrates a fascinating contradiction. The XKSS has become so valuable that its original purpose, being driven hard, can now represent a substantial financial risk. Yet treating it only as an investment seems contrary to everything that made the car remarkable. These machines were born from competition. They were built to accelerate, brake, change direction, and reward the person behind the wheel. The terrible irony of the XKSS is that its greatest modern enemy may not be fire or mechanical failure, but preservation. A racing car kept permanently motionless is a masterpiece denied part of its purpose.

16 Reasons to Remember

The E-Type deserves every accolade it has received. It was beautiful, innovative, fast, and, in its earliest form, surprisingly affordable next to the exotic machinery it challenged. It brought the essence of Jaguar’s racing heritage to thousands upon thousands of people who could never hope to own a D-Type, and that achievement should never be underestimated. The E-Type democratized a kind of automotive beauty that had previously belonged largely to the wealthy and the privileged. The XKSS did not. It was impossibly exclusive from the beginning.

But exclusivity was never the reason for its beauty. The XKSS emerged from the simple, brutally honest requirements of speed. Its body was shaped by airflow. Its structure was dictated by strength and weight. Its engine was chosen for power, durability, and efficiency, and its cockpit was designed around the driver rather than the expectations of a showroom customer. The result was an automobile that seemed almost incapable of dishonesty, where every surface expressed what lay beneath it and every mechanical detail revealed something about its purpose. And somehow, without trying to be glamorous, it became one of the most glamorous automobiles ever built. The E-Type is the Jaguar that conquered the world. The XKSS is the Jaguar that never needed to.

Some cars are remembered because they sold in enormous numbers. Others are remembered because they transformed an industry, established a new technology, or dominated an era of motorsport. The Jaguar XKSS occupies a different place in automotive history. It is remembered because it represents a moment when virtually everything aligned: an exceptional racing chassis, one of the greatest straight-six engines ever built, an aerodynamicist whose understanding of form was decades ahead of his contemporaries, and a company confident enough to put a genuine Le Mans machine on the road. And all of it wore a design of such breathtaking beauty that it remains almost impossible to believe it was created primarily through engineering necessity. Then came the fire, the rarity, the racing victories, and Steve McQueen, and those events turned a brilliant automobile into a legend.

But strip away the Hollywood association, the auction results, the sheer rarity, and even the tragic history, and something essential remains. The XKSS would still be magnificent, and that is perhaps the greatest compliment one can pay it.

There will always be arguments over the most beautiful Jaguar. Some will choose the E-Type, with its flowing hood and incomparable elegance. Others will prefer the purity of the C-Type, the drama of the D-Type, or the restrained sophistication of Jaguar’s great sedans. Even Frankel, who plainly loves the XKSS, rates it a shade less lovely than the D-Type it was built from. But the XKSS occupies a place all its own. It represents that exceedingly rare moment when beauty was not a styling objective. It was the unavoidable result of making something extraordinarily good at what it was designed to do.

The E-Type may be the most famous beautiful Jaguar. The XKSS may simply be the most beautiful. And somewhere in that distinction lies the entire magic of the car.
